the effect of selenium (Se) source and dose on the Se metabolism and status of horses.
the effects of dietary Se on the selenium status of horses.
the effect of dietary Se source and dose on the Se and thyroid hormone status of mature horses and the effect of Se source and dose of Se on the performance of horses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Se yeast was more efficient than Na selenate in increasing the Se status of mature horses, but it did no modify the GPX-1 status of these animals.
Se yeast supplementation increased the Se status of mature horses in a dose-dependent manner, but this was not associated with an increased GPX-1 response.
the Se yeast was more bioavailable than the inorganic Se source, as reflected by a greater Se concentration in blood and plasma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

SeMet is the predominant form of Se present in blood and plasma, but its concentration in blood is not directly correlated with GPX-1, and therefore the Se source is not important in the determination of the Se status of mature horses, as long as a minimum dose of 0.2 mg of total Se/d is provided.
the use of Se yeast as source of Se in mature horses is a viable option to enhance Se status.
horses supplemented with 0.2 mg of total Se as organic Se (SeMet) per kg of DM showed an adequate status of Se.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of Se yeast is an effective way to increase Se in blood and that this increase is mainly due to the greater proportion of Se as SeMet.
Se yeast is a good alternative for Se supplementation in horses.
Se yeast is a more efficient source than Na selenate for increasing the proportion of Se in the form of SeMet in blood, which may have a positive effect on Se bioavailability.
